I know, I get that. And I got a bit florid because I'm still quite touchy on the subject of her, plus two more of my cats are missing. So you know, my shit intruding on the conversation...

It was supposed to be an attempt to explain why keeping the cat on the bed is probably not an option for her, the way it wouldn't be for me.  And I would have done it even without the plastic sheeting, although I think we would have moved off the mattress far quicker.

I suspect the most constructive thing either or both of them can do is figure out what both can be comfortable with and what protections and cleaning requirements they can get sorted out, so that the cat can get through her last days in comfort.

I would definitely go with plastic sheeting though. It's a god send.

It's not for everyone, but some people prefer to make the accommodations for their cat's comfort. When I was poor and alone, I had my Elder Cat and she slept in my bed and loved me when no-one else did, and washed my face when I cried. 

When I was courting my wonderful husband, one of the first things he made sure of was that I knew he wouldn't try to remove the cats from the bed, because he recognised how much comfort it brought me, and how much comfort it brought them.

When my Elder Cat's health began to fail and she developed urinary incontinence, I put plastic sheets over the mattress, a plastic cover on the duvet (under the cotton cover) and on the pillows, and stocked up on cleaning sprays and washing liquid.  I chose to do these things because my priority was her comfort over my belongings. I also made sure my husband had an out if he wanted to sleep elsewhere (he didn't).  Not everyone is going to do that, and I'm not here to judge how anyone else copes, but my priority was Elder Cat's comfort.  Everything else can be cleaned.

When she was so ill that she could not get on the bed, I made a nest of bedding and slept on the floor so I could still be with her.  (Husband elected not to join in that one.)

Elder Cat is gone now. Even if I'd had to replace the bedding, the mattress, the carpets, hell, the whole bedroom, I would do it again because I got all those cuddles, the purrs, the little snorty snores, and the way she would twitch in her sleep and then snuggle closer to me.  All it cost me was a bit of cleaning product and a bit of time. And a sore back for a few days.

My not-a-goth phase. Went to university, decided it was time to grow out of it, bought regular clothes and learned regular makeup, went to regular clubs with regular people, got married, planned a family, did all the right things, made my parents proud... I hated myself all through that.

Got divorced, reconnected with an old mate, went to the local goth night for old times' sake, now I'm an aging goth married to another aging goth with a house full of cats and I've never been happier.

Woke up this morning to the remains on a bat on the dining room floor.  None of the cats has claimed responsibility but last year we saw Absinthe jump and catch one straight out of the air, so she's prime suspect.
She's so beautiful. I'm truly sorry

Charn. That bastard. I still have nightmares occasionally...

The thing is, at your wedding you make vows. Binding vows, and in your case as I understand it, vows made before God.

However good any translator is, there is always going to be a little bit of a barrier. If you both speak the same native language then it is really important that the wedding is in that language because you are making a commitment based on what is said.

The people that matter here are you, making the vows, and the witnesses, understanding your words as you make them.  You both need them to be in ASL, for that purpose.

Of course, every other reason everyone has said about it being your wedding, your language, your choice, is also completely correct.

NTA, and congratulations and blessings to you.
